claim: Robots can grasp a wide variety of flat objects (books, plates, boxes, boards, towels) lying on a table, including objects and whole categories never seen in training, if the task is split into first choosing one of a few manipulation strategies from the object's point cloud (push it to the table edge, lift it with two arms, or squeeze up a fold for soft items) and then executing that strategy as a sequence of short learned motion primitives, rather than learning a single strategy or an end-to-end policy. Supported only if, in simulation with five trials per object, its grasp success on unseen objects of seen categories and on objects of unseen categories is higher than each fixed-strategy method and each end-to-end policy (2D and 3D diffusion policies, OpenVLA, pi0, pi0.5), by at least 15 points on the unseen categories; if end-to-end vision-language-action policies lose most of their training-set success on unseen objects while this approach loses little; and if on a physical dual-arm robot it grasps at least 75% of unseen-category objects.

experiments: Build the simulation benchmark and splits. Setup: Isaac Sim 4.5 with two 7-DoF Franka arms, RMPFlow control, 104 flat objects in 21 categories with empirical mass, friction and texture, deformable objects simulated with GPU position-based dynamics, 18 scenes; automated collection of point clouds and gripper poses from randomised trials labelled by a success criterion (object held aloft without slipping for 2 s). Split objects into Train, Test-alpha (unseen objects of training categories) and Test-beta (unseen categories). Label each object with a strategy: push to the table edge (thin, small), two-arm cooperative lift (thick, large) or edge squeezing (deformable).

Define the two-stage method. Setup: a PointNet-style strategy classifier on the object's own point cloud, trained with cross-entropy plus a contrastive loss whose positives share a strategy but come from different objects and whose negatives come from the same object relabelled with another strategy; training data expanded to 1,390 point clouds by rescaling objects to seven sizes and converting deformable assets to rigid ones (changing their label). Each strategy is executed as a sequence of primitives (touch, slide, squeeze, lift), each a start and end gripper pose predicted from the scene point cloud by a PointNet++ encoder with separate position and rotation heads (squared position error plus quaternion geodesic loss), trained on 50 automatic demonstrations per object.

Compare with fixed-strategy and end-to-end methods. Setup: five trials per object over all 104 objects with randomised placement; baselines: slide-to-edge only, two-arm lift only, Diffusion Policy, 3D Diffusion Policy, OpenVLA, pi0 and pi0.5 trained end to end. Result: success on Train / Test-alpha / Test-beta 81.1 / 74.2 / 69.0% against 66.2 / 54.2 / 51.2% for 3D Diffusion Policy (best baseline), 68.6 / 28.6 / 25.0% for pi0.5, 63.0 / 23.6 / 17.3% for pi0, 55.5 / 22.6 / 17.8% for OpenVLA, 48.8 / 36.8 / 38.8% for Diffusion Policy, and 32.3 / 27.3 / 24.7% and 41.2 / 35.0 / 27.2% for the fixed strategies. Per object, pushing works for books and disks but fails for boxes and fabric, lifting the reverse, while the two-stage method is competitive on most objects; 3D Diffusion Policy matches or beats it on a few soft items (skirt 15/20 vs 13/20, fabric 9/10 vs 7/10 in training).

Separate strategy choice from execution. Setup: strategy-classification accuracy and grasp success per object and split. Result: strategy accuracy 99.2% / 91.3% / 78.6% on Train / Test-alpha / Test-beta in the main evaluation (92.1% / 82.6% / 75.8% in the per-trial count); failures concentrate on irregular unseen shapes (laptop 5/10, chessboard 13/20, painting 14/20) and on wrong strategy choices, e.g. lifting where pushing was needed.

Ablate the inputs and training aids. Setup: strategy accuracy and grasp-position error with RGB instead of the object point cloud, with the whole scene's point cloud, without scale and material augmentation, without the contrastive loss, without both, without primitive decomposition, and without the rotation loss. Result (Test-beta strategy accuracy): RGB input 56.4%, scene point cloud 70.5%, no augmentation 71.4%, neither augmentation nor contrastive loss 70.5%, no contrastive loss 77.3%, against 78.6% for the full model; without primitive decomposition the grasp-position error rises from 0.0040 to 0.0076-0.0114 on Test-beta, and without the rotation loss to 0.0077.

Test long-horizon clearing, other datasets and a real robot. Setup: (a) clear a cluttered table of five unseen objects from different categories, comparing against GPT-4o choosing strategies with the same primitive library; (b) evaluate on the public GraspLargeFlat, PreAfford and AdaptPNP object sets; (c) a Baxter dual-arm robot with a RealSense D455 and SAM segmentation on more than 30 real flat objects split the same way. Result: (a) 73.3% vs 36.7% for GPT-4o; (b) 80.7%, 82.5% and 84.0%; (c) 83.6% / 80.0% / 80.0% on Train / Test-alpha / Test-beta, higher than in simulation, which the authors attribute to more stable real friction and more easily formed folds in real fabric.

Check sensitivity to the loss weights. Setup: vary the contrastive weight and temperature of the strategy classifier and the position-loss weight (1-20) with rotation weight fixed. Result: very small contrastive weights lower test accuracy markedly while a broad middle range is stable; position error is lowest at weights 5-10 (Test-beta 0.0040 vs 0.0058 at weight 1) and rotation error barely changes.
